title: Generators and paralleling
where: the Electrical shelf's Power and machines folder
folderRuns: Motors, Generators and paralleling, HV Subsea Cable Testing
blurb: How an alternator makes its voltage, the AVR and the governor, synchronising, load sharing and reverse power.
from: any Brilliant electricity or electromagnetism course still reachable on brilliant.org, and failing that the nearest public course on synchronous machines
others: Hughes Electrical and Electronic Technology and Bird's Electrical Circuit Theory and Technology (synchronous machine chapters, contents), public generator manufacturers' application guides (Cummins, Caterpillar, Leroy-Somer, Stamford/Cummins AvK, Woodward on governors and load sharing, Deep Sea Electronics or ComAp on synchronising), and OpenLearn or university lecture notes on synchronous generators
syllabi: What a marine electrical engineer actually uses of this topic: the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) and A-III/1 competence lines that touch it, the MCA electro-technical officer and engineer officer syllabus lines (Electrotechnology), the public apprenticeship standards for an electrical or marine engineering technician on the Institute for Apprenticeships site, and the Pearson BTEC HN units that cover it. Exact lines. Also what Dan's electrical qualifications and the built Motors course already cover
scope: Synchronous generators and running them in parallel, from first principles, in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) the alternator: a rotating field on the rotor, three stator windings, frequency from speed and poles (f = pn/60), and the EMF rising with field current and speed (AC circuits lesson 1 built the turning coil: use it; Transformers and magnetism, built just before this course, taught Faraday's law, flux and magnetic circuits: build on them, never re-teach them); (2) excitation and the AVR: how field current sets the voltage, brushless exciters, and how the AVR holds voltage as load changes; (3) the loaded generator: armature reaction and synchronous reactance, the phasor diagram E = V + jXI, and why a lagging load needs more excitation (AC circuits built phasors and power factor: use them); (4) the governor: the prime mover sets real power and frequency, droop and isochronous control, and what a sudden load step does (Mechanics and materials built torque, inertia and run-up: use them); (5) synchronising: the four conditions (voltage, frequency, phase sequence, phase angle), the synchroscope and lamps, check-synchronising, and what a bad closure does; (6) load sharing: kW shared by governor droop settings, kVAr shared by AVR droop or cross-current compensation, and why they are separate; (7) protection and faults: reverse power, loss of excitation, overcurrent and short-circuit decrement, preference tripping and load shedding; (8) the generator in a power system: starting a big motor (voltage dip), blackout and restoration in outline, and the diesel generator as a whole (Heat and fluids built the engine's energy split: use it). General marine and industrial diesel generator sets only. Examples from public, general marine and industrial equipment only; never how the Royal Navy or a particular boat does it, never submarine systems beyond CLAUDE.md's public outline, and never anything from Dan's SMQ books.
